Free Public Records Tools

Two free helpers for finding the right office and asking an agency for records. Both run in your browser, and nothing you type is sent to us or stored.

Which Office Has the Record?

Records are split between many offices. Pick what you are looking for to see where it is usually kept and which guides explain the search.

Start with

The Clerk of Court (county or state), or PACER for federal cases

What it holds: Dockets, filings, judgments, and orders for cases filed in that court.

Tip: Start with the county where the case was filed. Federal and state courts keep separate records.

Start with

The County Recorder or Register of Deeds, plus the Assessor

What it holds: The recorder keeps deeds, mortgages, liens, and releases. The assessor lists the owner on the tax roll and the assessed value.

Tip: Search by parcel number when you can. Addresses and owner names are easy to mismatch.

Read next

  • How to Find Property Records and Liens in Your County
  • County Clerk vs. Recorder vs. Assessor: Who Holds Which Records?

Start with

The County Treasurer or Tax Collector

What it holds: Tax bills, payments, delinquent amounts, and tax sale status.

Tip: Also look for a recorded tax lien at the recorder’s office.

Read next

  • County Clerk vs. Recorder vs. Assessor: Who Holds Which Records?
  • How to Find Property Records and Liens in Your County

Start with

The Secretary of State (business filing office) in the state where it was formed

What it holds: Entity status, formation date, registered agent, and annual report filings.

Tip: Check the state of formation and any state where the company does business.

Read next

  • Understanding LLC Filings: How to Conduct Proper Business Entity Searches
  • The Importance of Registered Agents in Business Filings

Start with

Several sources used together

What it holds: Secretary of State filings, liens and UCC records, court dockets, bankruptcy filings, and licensing boards.

Tip: Keep a log of each check with the source and the date.

Read next

  • How to Conduct Due Diligence on a New Business Partner

Start with

The U.S. Bankruptcy Court, searchable through PACER

What it holds: Petitions, schedules, trustee reports, and discharge or dismissal orders.

Tip: Look for a discharge order to see how a case ended.

Read next

  • How to Search Bankruptcy Records Using the PACER System
  • Understanding Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 Bankruptcy Filings

Start with

The state contractor or professional licensing board

What it holds: License status, classification, expiration date, and any discipline.

Tip: Confirm the license class covers the kind of work you are hiring for.

Read next

  • How to Verify a Contractor's Business License and Protect Your Investment

Start with

The state Department of Corrections (prison) or the county Sheriff (jail)

What it holds: Inmate locators and jail rosters showing custody status.

Tip: Federal inmates are in a separate system run by the Bureau of Prisons.

Read next

  • How to Find Incarceration Records and Inmate Status by State
  • The Critical Difference Between State and Federal Inmate Searches

Start with

The state registry and the National Sex Offender Public Website

What it holds: Registered offender listings, with the details shown varying by state.

Tip: Registry information is for safety purposes, not for harassment.

Read next

  • Navigating the National Sex Offender Public Website (NSOPW)

Start with

The office that holds the original record

What it holds: Certified or exemplified copies for official use.

Tip: Ask the agency that will receive it exactly what kind of certification it needs.

Read next

  • How to Request Certified Copies of Public Records

Start with

A public records request: FOIA for federal agencies, your state’s law for state and local ones

What it holds: Agency contracts, emails, reports, and other records that are not already published.

Tip: Be specific about the records you want and the date range.

Start with

The office that publishes the record, plus any address confidentiality program you qualify for

What it holds: Court dockets, property records, and business filings can show names and addresses.

Tip: Ask the custodian about redaction, and ask a legal aid office about sealing.

This is a template, not legal advice. Deadlines, fees, and exemptions differ by state, so check the law that applies to your request.

How the Office Finder Works

County and state governments are organized differently, so the finder shows the office that usually holds each type of record, not a guarantee. It follows the common roles explained in our guide to county clerks, recorders, and assessors. If your county uses different names, search the county website for the record type, such as "deed search" or "marriage license," or call the main county line and ask who handles it.

Using Your Request Letter

  1. Find the right office. Federal agencies list a FOIA contact on their websites, and FOIA.gov has a directory. For state and local records, look for the agency's public records officer or custodian.
  2. Edit the letter. Replace any bracketed text and make the description of the records as specific as you can. Narrow requests are answered faster.
  3. Send it and keep a copy. Use the agency's online portal or email if it has one. Save the date you sent it and any tracking number you receive.
  4. Follow up. Federal agencies generally have 20 business days to respond to a FOIA request. State deadlines differ, so check your state's law.
  5. Know your options. If the request is denied, the agency must explain how to appeal. Our beginner's guide to FOIA requests covers exemptions, fees, and appeals.

Good to Know

These tools provide general information and a starting template, not legal advice. The letter is generic, so review it before sending, and check the rules that apply in your state or agency.
